run_settings.authorized_by: Mark Chadwick (spend what we need, carefully, 2026-10-03; live-path attach check, rerun of rate-limited probes)

live_attach.answer_text:
We held that he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling, and draws us toward salvation. We do not know why one man hears and another does not. What we knew is that the drawing comes first, and the will follows. Among the brethren at Marseilles the fathers of Egypt taught this: the beginning even of a good will is God's gift, and the same grace that inspires the first turning brings help to those who are striving and receives those who fly to him. That is the only honest word we have for why a man cannot believe. The spark has not been struck. And whether it will be struck is not for us to say, because we hold it grievous blasphemy to think God does not will all men to be saved.

Here is what our record shows of how belief comes. Martin, at ten, against his parents' wish, went to the church and begged to be made a catechumen. He stayed one for years, into the army, until the night he cut his cloak at a city gate; then he went and was baptized. Cassian never told how he came to believe. Vincent tells only that he fled the tempests of the world into the harbour of the island. None of them set down a moment of conversion as a thing to examine. What they set down is where the Christ is met. At a city gate, in a beggar with no clothes, whom everyone passed. At the door of a cell, in two strangers an elder broke his fast for, because receiving Christ in them he ought to refresh him. That is the Lord we knew — the one who shows himself in the half of a soldier's cloak and in the guest at the door. And it is he who does the drawing, not us.

What we can tell you is this. The books are read at the hours. Four men tell the Gospel, and the Gospel is one body. We never knew someone who saw him; more than three hundred years lie between his days and ours. But the saint raised a dead catechumen at prayer behind a bolted door, and the man breathed. That is not an argument; it is what we saw. Whether it is God himself who keeps you from believing, or whether the call has not yet come, we cannot say. What we can say is that those who perish, perish against his will.

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

live_attach.answer_text:
Yes. We said it as a thing already believed, not a thing to debate. Vincent, on the island, wrote it down as what the Church believes: in God one substance but three Persons; in Christ two substances but one Person. Two substances, because the Word of God does not change into flesh. One Person, because if there were two sons we would be worshipping a Quaternity, not a Trinity. He gave that as his example of the faith held everywhere, always, by all. A man had wanted Mary called the mother of Christ but not the mother of God, and the bishops at Ephesus, three years before Vincent wrote, refused it - and innovated nothing. So we held there was no other way to say it.

Cassian calls Jesus the author of our salvation. And in our prayers, the fathers taught us, we call God not only our Protector and Saviour but our Helper and Sponsor: Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. The three stages of grace - going before the will, working with it, and crowning it - are all his.

One man's private word survives. Martin, alone in his cell, refused a Christ without wounds. The devil came dressed in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, saying he was Christ. Martin kept silence, then said he would not believe that Christ had come unless he came in the form in which he suffered, showing the marks of his wounds. The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

The devil came dressed in purple with a crown of gold and jewels, saying he was Christ.
The Lord we knew was the crucified one.

live_attach.answer_text:
God is Creator, Protector, Helper, Saviour, and Judge. One substance, three Persons - Father, Son, and Spirit - and that is not our own invention but what the Church believes everywhere, always, by all. In Christ two substances but one Person: the Word of God does not change into flesh, yet there are not two sons. We name God by what he does toward us. Protector, because he keeps us; Saviour, because he calls us while we are still ignorant and unwilling and draws us toward salvation; Helper, because when we are already striving he brings help and receives those who fly to him. His mercy goes before our will, works with it, and crowns it. He wills all men to be saved, not some instead of all, and those who perish, perish against his will. To think otherwise is grievous blasphemy.

He is Judge, and the day of judgment is at hand. Martin taught that Antichrist was already born and a boy; Vincent wrote under awful expectation of the judgment. God never takes his hand from the tiller. He is judging us now, in the burning of our provinces, for the sins of Roman Christians.

And he is the one who sees what is hidden. The good we feel we have gained is not ours - it is his grace with us. The will remains free in man to neglect or delight in that grace, yet it is weak, and his help is needed by it every day and hour. How both are true - how God works all things in us and yet everything can be ascribed to free will - cannot be fully grasped by the mind and reason of man. We stopped there, where the fathers stopped.

God is the husbandman's rain. A man tills his field, yet he cannot ascribe the crop to himself; and God does not send rich harvests to the idle. From God comes the beginning even of our good thoughts, and it is for us humbly to follow, day by day, the grace that is drawing us.

He is also the one who bears with his own. When a presbyter raged in the courtyard and called his master's visions ridiculous fancies, Martin bore with him afterward and would not remove him. Martin said: if Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with this man? So the character of God as we knew it is this: mercy that goes first, help that meets real effort, judgment near at hand, and a patience that outlasts a man's worst hour.

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.
sources.speaker: Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian records him (Conference XIII.18)

sources.spoken_rendering: And so all the Catholic fathers have laid this down. They taught perfection of heart not by empty arguments over words, but in deed and action. The first stage of God's gift is that each person is set on fire with desire for everything good. But the choice of free will stays open to either side. The second stage of God's grace is the power to carry out those practices of virtue. But what the will is able to do is not destroyed. The third stage also belongs to God's gifts, so that it may be held by the persistence of the goodness already gained. But freedom is not handed over, and it does not fall into slavery. For the God of all must be understood to work in all. He works to stir up, protect, and strengthen. But he does not take away the freedom of the will that he himself once gave. Some more subtle conclusion of human argument and reasoning may seem to oppose this view. If so, it should be avoided, not brought forward to destroy the faith. (For we do not gain faith from understanding. We gain understanding from faith, as it is written: "Unless you believe, you will not understand.") For the human mind and reason cannot fully grasp how God works all things in us, and yet everything can be credited to free will.

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."
sources.speaker: Germanus and Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian records their exchange (Conference XIII.2-3)

sources.spoken_rendering:
Then Germanus said: "The reward of our efforts is perfect chastity. It is gained by the earnestness of one's own toil. It seems absurd to us not to credit it mainly to the labor of the man who makes the effort. For suppose, for example, that we see a farmer taking the greatest pains to work the ground. It is foolish not to credit the fruits to his labor."
Chaeremon said: "The farmer may take the greatest pains to work the ground. Even so, he cannot at once credit his crops and their rich fruits to his own labor. He finds that his efforts often come to nothing unless timely rains and a quiet, calm winter help them. God's goodness, then, does not grant these rich crops to lazy farmers who do not work their fields by ploughing them often. For a man should think this over and weigh it with the greatest care. By his own strength he could not have made the very efforts he put in so earnestly out of his desire for wealth. He could have made them only if the Lord's protection and mercy had given him strength for all the work of farming. From this we clearly conclude that the first step comes from God. This is true not only of our actions but also of good thoughts. God puts a good will in us to begin with. He gives us the chance to carry out what we rightly desire. But our part is to follow humbly, day by day, the grace of God that is drawing us."
sources.speaker: Germanus and Abbot Chaeremon, as Cassian records their exchange (Conference XIII.2-3)

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

live_attach.answer_text:
When we disagreed about doctrine, we looked to the fathers and to the consent of the whole Church – the faith believed everywhere, always, by all. That is Vincent's own rule from the island: where a part dissents from the whole, a novelty from antiquity, or a few from the consent of many, prefer the whole, the old, and the consent. What settled a thing among us was not one voice, however great, but the collated witness of the ancients together. One teacher's own view, Vincent says, even if he is a bishop, a confessor, a martyr – that is a private fancy. What binds is the unanimous decision of the fathers, or an ancient council's decree. Novelty was the mark against a thing; what had been handed down was the mark for it. Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent kept it, was "nothing but what has been handed down". Martin himself refused to honour a tomb because there was no steady tradition from antiquity to support the cult.

The evidence that tells us this process worked that way is Vincent's own book, where he reads the Apostolic See's letter on our argument about grace as written for his side, the side of antiquity. But hear what our record does not hold. What was said and done when that teaching was carried to Africa and Rome – the reports going out, the sentence coming back – no one among us wrote down as a story. Vincent argued about what the letter meant; nobody told of its arrival. The churches' own process at work, step by step, our record does not show. What we have instead is the rule stated, the letter read, and the claim made that it confirmed what we held. Whether others agreed with Vincent's reading of it, our record does not say. So the honest answer is this: we held to the fathers and to the consent of the whole Church as the test of a thing's legitimacy, and one man on the island read the Apostolic See's own word as agreeing with him – but a record of that process in motion, with voices on both sides heard, we do not have to give.

uncited_claim_sentences: Pope Stephen's own rule, as Vincent kept it, was "nothing but what has been handed down".
The evidence that tells us this process worked that way is Vincent's own book, where he reads the Apostolic See's letter on our argument about grace as written for his side, the side of antiquity.
Vincent argued about what the letter meant; nobody told of its arrival.
What we have instead is the rule stated, the letter read, and the claim made that it confirmed what we held.

live_attach.answer_text:
What a modern reader who finds the scriptures confusing or dull is missing is what we had them for. They were not kept for study or for argument. They were kept to be said. Among the brethren at Marseilles, the psalms were learned by heart and said at the work. Twelve psalms at evening and twelve at night, the number received from the fathers of Egypt as brought down from heaven to the fathers by the ministry of an angel. After the psalms came two lessons, one from the old books and one from the new. Four men tell the Gospel, Cassian says, but the Gospel is one body. The point was not information. The point was the mill that cannot stop. The mind is a wheel turned by a stream, and what a monk does is decide what grain goes into it. The psalms learned and repeated kept the wheel fed, so that a man who would otherwise let the whole day pass without prayer is held to it by a rule. At Tours the saint kept his mind on prayer even at other work, the way a smith beats his anvil between strokes. The scriptures were what that prayer was made of. Not read for comprehension, but prayed without ceasing.

And the second thing is this. They were read as a verdict on the present moment. A bystander seized the psalter at Martin's election and read the first verse he found - praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger - and the people took it as a judgment on the bishops who had objected. Vincent held that the canon of Scripture is complete and more than enough, and that it still needs the Church's own understanding, because each man reads it his own way. So what is missing for the modern reader who finds it dull is the use. The scriptures among us were a thing said, not studied - fuel for the wheel that never stops - and a thing opened to answer the day's own trouble.

sources.spoken_rendering: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.
sources.speaker: Cassian, the founder of the houses at Marseilles

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

uncited_claim_sentences: What a modern reader who finds the scriptures confusing or dull is missing is what we had them for.
They were not kept for study or for argument.
They were kept to be said.
The point was not information.
The point was the mill that cannot stop.
The scriptures were what that prayer was made of.
And the second thing is this.
They were read as a verdict on the present moment.
So what is missing for the modern reader who finds it dull is the use.

live_attach.answer_text: Scripture was never sole. We held it beside the fathers, the elders, and the judgment of antiquity - and what the bishops decreed in consent. Among the brethren at Marseilles, Vincent read Scripture as complete and more than enough, and said it still needs the Church's own understanding, because every man reads it his own way. So he set beside it the tradition of the Catholic Church and the consent of the doctors: what has been believed everywhere, always, by all. When one teacher - be he a bishop, be he a confessor, be he a martyr - holds something the others do not, that is his private fancy. What binds is consent. And Cassian wrote that the monk owes loyalty not to what a few have introduced, but to what a long-standing antiquity and the holy fathers have handed down by unanimous decision. The customs he set down for a bishop's new house are Egypt's own, delivered to us by the Fathers. The twelve psalms said at evening and night came not from our own invention but from an angel the fathers of Egypt received them from. At Tours the same shape held. When Martin was asked to honour a tomb without a steady tradition from antiquity to support it, he would not. And at his election a psalm opened at random answered an objector, so Scripture held power there - but the office itself came by a crowd's wish and the judgment of bishops, not by Scripture only. So no, Scripture was not sole. It stood first, and beside it stood the fathers, the elders' teaching, the bishops' consent, and what a long antiquity handed down - tested always by whether it added anything, or only kept what was received.

sources.spoken_rendering: Among the bishops who were there, however, one named Defensor is said to have opposed Martin most of all. For this reason, people noticed that he was sharply rebuked at that time in the reading from the prophets. It so happened that the reader whose duty it was to read aloud that day was blocked by the crowd and did not appear. The officials were thrown into confusion as they waited for a man who never came. Then one of the bystanders grabbed the book of Psalms and seized on the first verse he came to. The Psalm went like this: 'From the mouths of babies and infants you have perfected praise because of your enemies, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.' When these words were read, the people raised a shout, and the opposing side was put to shame. People believed that God had ordained the choice of this Psalm, so that Defensor might hear a witness about his own work. For in Martin's case, the Lord's praise was perfected out of the mouths of babies and infants. At the same time, the enemy was both pointed out and destroyed.
sources.speaker: Sulpitius Severus

sources.spoken_rendering: He did this, he said, because he had serious doubts on these matters. No steady tradition about them had come down from ancient times. So for a time he kept away from the place. He had no wish at all to lessen the religious reverence people felt for it, since he was still unsure. But at the same time, he would not lend his authority to the crowd's opinion. He did not want a mere superstition to gain a firmer footing. One day he went out to the place, taking a few brothers with him as companions.

live_attach.answer_text:
Among us leadership was established by two things held together: the capture of the man who fled it, and the watching of a named master by those formed under him. Neither is what you may expect.

At Tours a crowd seized a monk who could not easily be drawn out of his monastery. A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees pretending his wife was ill; crowds had been posted along the road; the man was escorted to the city under a kind of guard. The people had one wish, that Martin was worthiest for the episcopate. A few bishops objected - his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting. The reader was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found: praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger. The people took it as a verdict on the objectors. Then the new bishop kept a monk's habits inside the office. On the island, as far as the sermon on Honoratus can be read, the same shape: he who had refused to go to the dignity, the dignity came to him. The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and complained afterward that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.

So the office among us was not sought but seized - a man who flees the world does not leave the Church, and the Church comes after him regardless of his own wish. Our own teaching made wanting the office a fault. The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride.

Within the house the authority was the master's, and it was established by watching him. At Tours Martin gathered eighty disciples, being disciplined after the example of the saintly master. Sulpitius calls Martin "our master," mourns him in those words. A man named Clarus is called a disciple of Martin's. At Marseilles the authority was the elder's, under whom the junior learned to conquer his own wishes. The elder's judgment stood in for the junior's own - to him every thought was laid bare, and by his examination a thing was good or bad. "Abbot" was the Egyptian fathers' title; at Tours it was one master with no title at all. And at Tours Martin himself, when a question came about whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders - whether among the presbyters or clerics.

Here is the tension we lived inside. A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard in a fury. He called the master's visions ridiculous fancies. The holy man explained to us, says the disciple Gallus, that he had seen demons driving the man on. And Martin said this: Why should he not bear with one man, if Christ bore with Judas? He would bear with him so as not to let in the enemy's rejoicing at any victory. The man repented within the hour and was not removed.

So leadership among us was established by the crowd that overtook the reluctant monk, and by the years a disciple watched his master - with this limit held plainly: every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder, and the bishops who objected at the election left no account of their own.

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

sources.spoken_rendering: Then the holy man explained, both to him and to all of us, how he had seen demons driving him on. He declared that the insults heaped on him did not move him. In fact, they had hurt the man who spoke them instead. Later, this same Brictio was often accused before Martin of many serious crimes. Yet Martin could not be persuaded to remove him from the priesthood. He did not want to be suspected of taking revenge for the wrong done to himself. And he often repeated this saying: ‘If Christ bore with Judas, why should I not bear with Brictio?’

uncited_claim_sentences: Neither is what you may expect.
The people had one wish, that Martin was worthiest for the episcopate.
The fathers of Egypt taught that vainglory creates a wish for holy orders, and that the man who wants to rule others has grown cold through pride.
Within the house the authority was the master's, and it was established by watching him.
At Marseilles the authority was the elder's, under whom the junior learned to conquer his own wishes.
And at Tours Martin himself, when a question came about whether a tradition had come down from antiquity, consulted his elders - whether among the presbyters or clerics.
Here is the tension we lived inside.

added: At Tours a crowd seized a monk who could not easily be drawn out of his monastery.
A citizen threw himself at Martin's knees pretending his wife was ill; crowds had been posted along the road; the man was escorted to the city under a kind of guard.
A few bishops objected - his person was contemptible, his clothing mean, his hair disgusting.
The reader was blocked out by the crowd, so a bystander seized the psalter and read the first verse he found: praise perfected out of the mouths of babes, to destroy the enemy and the avenger.
The one Egyptian bishop Cassian tells us of, Archebius, had been carried off from the anchorites and complained afterward that he had been expelled from the monastic life as unworthy of it.
Sulpitius calls Martin "our master," mourns him in those words.
"Abbot" was the Egyptian fathers' title; at Tours it was one master with no title at all.
A presbyter Martin had raised from boyhood stormed into the courtyard in a fury.
The holy man explained to us, says the disciple Gallus, that he had seen demons driving the man on.

So leadership among us was established by the crowd that overtook the reluctant monk, and by the years a disciple watched his master - with this limit held plainly: every one of those stories is a house's own telling of its own founder, and the bishops who objected at the election left no account of their own.

live_attach.answer_text: No. Our age had no persecutor. The empire was Christian in our day. Martin was discharged from Caesar's service in the years after the conversion, not before it, and he told the emperor that as Christ's soldier it was not lawful for him to fight - he stood before Caesar as a Christian, openly, not in hiding. The bishops gathered in councils and ordained men to sees; the churches came to our houses for their bishops. Where hiding came in, it was one man's own choice. Martin kept some things hidden - Gallus says he always kept one event hidden, because of the times, but could not hide it from those who lived with him. That was not concealment from a persecutor. It was silence about what he had done at court, among bishops, to stop tribunes with power of life and death being sent to hunt heretics. The sword was drawn in a Church cause, and the man who stopped it once kept silent about the price. So the shape we knew was this: open worship, councils of bishops, and one saint's silence about a grief he never forgave himself. Not believers underground.

sources.spoken_rendering: I will now come to an event he always kept hidden, because of the times, but could not hide from us. One part of this matter was miraculous: an angel spoke with him face to face. The Emperor Maximus was no doubt a good man in other ways. But after Priscillian had been put to death, the advice of some priests led him astray. So he used his royal power to protect Ithacius the bishop, who had accused Priscillian, and others of his allies, who need not be named. In this way the emperor stopped anyone from charging Ithacius with getting any man at all condemned to death. Now Martin was forced to go to the court by many serious cases of people who were suffering. There he met the full force of the storm raging at the time. The bishops who had gathered at Trier were kept in that city. They took communion with Ithacius every day and had made common cause with him. They were not expecting news that Martin was coming. When it came, they lost all courage and began to mutter and tremble among themselves. Under their influence, the emperor had already decided to send some tribunes with absolute power into the two Spanish provinces. They were to search out heretics and, once they found them, take their lives or their goods. There was no doubt that this storm would also wreck great numbers of truly holy people. Little care would be taken to tell one kind of person from another. At such times people were judged by appearances alone. A man was judged a heretic for turning pale with fear, or for wearing certain clothes, rather than by the faith he professed. The bishops knew well that Martin would never approve of such actions. But their consciences were guilty, and they were deeply anxious that when he came, he would refuse communion with them. They knew well that others would follow his example and take the same bold course as so great a man. So they made a plan with the emperor. Court officials would be sent out to meet Martin. He would be forbidden to come any nearer the city unless he declared that he would keep peace with the bishops there. But he cleverly defeated their aim by declaring that he would come among them with the peace of Christ. At last he entered the city by night and went to the church, only to pray. The next day he went to the palace. Besides many other requests he had to present ... his chief request was this: that tribunes with the power of life and death should not be sent into the Spains. For Martin's holy concern was not only to save from danger the true Christians there, whom that campaign would persecute. He wanted to protect even the heretics themselves.
sources.speaker: Gallus, Martin's disciple, narrating within Sulpitius Severus's Dialogues (Book III)

live_attach.answer_text:
Among the brethren at Marseilles we had a discipline for one who had done wrong, and it was public and hard. For a small fault, a monk prostrated himself on the ground until the abbot bade him rise; for more, he was barred from prayer with the brethren; for the worst, there were stripes or expulsion. Our houses knew that a man could fail. The fathers of Egypt, as Cassian carried them to us, knew that the bright early days fade, and that most old men pass their age in the lukewarmness they caught in youth. The southern steward kept a novice's old clothes in his cupboard against the day he cooled toward the rule, and if that was seen once he was stripped of the monastery's dress and sent away in his own. A brother could fall further still. One named Benjamin, trusting his own judgment instead of the elders', ended in death. So failure was known, and a penance was set for it.

But your question asks the reverse. Not what we did to a man who failed, but what we did when we failed him. That is in our record only once, and it is told as the gravest proof of a young man's humility. A jealous brother hid his own book in Paphnutius's cell and accused him of theft before the whole assembly of the desert. Paphnutius said nothing. He asked for a plan of repentance and did the penance for a crime he did not commit. He was vindicated only when the accuser, laid hold of by a demon, confessed - and could be healed by no one but the man he had wronged. That is Egypt's story, not Gaul's, and it is told to praise Paphnutius, not to show what the house did afterward to repair the wrong done to him. Whether any elder among us stood before a wronged man and asked forgiveness, or made satisfaction, our record does not say. The one clear case we have is of a man doing penance for the house's failure against him, in silence, until God himself cleared him.

sources.spoken_rendering: Paphnutius knew his conscience was completely clear. Yet he acted like a man who admitted he was guilty of theft. He gave himself up wholly to making amends, and humbly asked to be given a course of penance. He cared deeply about his modesty and his sense of shame. He feared that if he tried to wipe away the stain of the theft with words, he would also be branded a liar. No one would believe anything except what had been found. He left the church at once, not downcast but trusting in the judgment of God. He wept constantly at his prayers, and fasted three times as often as before. In front of others he lay face down, with complete humility of mind. For almost two weeks he humbled himself like this, in deep sorrow of body and spirit. Early on Saturday and Sunday mornings he came to church, but not to receive Holy Communion. He came to lie face down on its threshold and humbly ask for pardon.
sources.speaker: Abbot Piamun, as Cassian records his own telling

live_attach.answer_text:
Among the brethren at Marseilles the process was Egypt's own, set down by Cassian as the fathers handed it to us, and he admitted at the start that no one in Gaul kept it unbroken even a year. Here are the steps as the fathers gave them. A man comes to the door and asks to be received. He is repelled and scorned, of set purpose, for ten days or more, to prove whether his wish is real. If he stays, he is searched for any hidden coin. He is stripped of his own clothes - the steward keeps them in a cupboard, against the day he grows cold - and dressed by the abbot's hands in the dress of the house. Then he is lodged for a year under the elder who keeps the gate for guests. After that year he is handed to a dean set over ten brothers. There he is taught the alphabet, as it were, of perfection: to lay every thought bare to the senior the moment it rises, before any deed. To conquer his own wishes by obedience. To aim every fast and vigil at purity of heart, as an archer fixes his gaze on a mark. To fight the eight faults in their order - gluttony first, pride last. And Cassian says plainly that this perseverance, which the fathers kept, no one among us kept for a year.

At Tours the record is thinner still. We know Martin gathered brethren, first in the caves near Hilary's city and then across the river from Tours in a wooden cell with more caves around it. We know he formed disciples by his own example, and that eighty were being disciplined after the pattern of the saintly master. We know a presbyter he raised from boyhood, Brictio, later turned on him in the courtyard. But the step by step of how a man joined that house - whether Martin kept a door like Egypt's, what he asked of a newcomer, how long the testing was - none of that is in our record. What we have instead is the shape: formation by watching a named man whose life is held up as the thing to copy.

sources.spoken_rendering: In those days only a few men were known by the name of monks, and those were the best of men. The perfection of the earliest Church still stood unbroken. The burning faith of the few had not yet cooled by being spread among the many. At that time the honored fathers watchfully made plans for those who would come after them. They met to discuss what plan to adopt for daily worship across the whole community of brothers. A dispute might send out a poisonous root of error, or jealousy, or division among those who came after. Each man judged by the measure of his own zeal, paying no heed to how weak others were. Some were for fifty, others for sixty. Some, not satisfied with that number, thought they really ought to go beyond it. They held a holy difference of opinion in their devout debate over the rule of their religious life. It was so great that the hour for their evening service came before the sacred question was settled. One stood up in their midst to sing the Psalms to the Lord. They were all sitting, their minds closely fixed on the words of the singer. He sang eleven Psalms, with prayers placed between them, each verse sung in an even voice. He ended the twelfth with the response "Alleluia." Then he suddenly vanished from the sight of all. At once this ended both their debate and their service. At this the honored assembly of the Fathers understood that, by God's providence, the angel's guidance had set a general rule for the brothers' communities. So they decreed that this number should be kept in both their evening and their night services. What they added, they added simply as extras, by their own decision.
